turns.content: Hey, quick question. I'm cataloging these closed mediation binders for Gary and the master log is incomplete. Some folders don't have case years and a few overlap on topics. Should I group by year or dispute type? Also, kind of wondering if Gary is benching me from the front desk because of those phone mess-ups yesterday.

Two very different questions, so let me take them one at a time.

**The binders:** I'd go year as the primary sort, dispute type as a secondary tag. Reasons:

- Closed files almost always get pulled for retention/destruction purposes, and retention schedules run on dates, not topics. Future-you (or future-Gary) will thank you.
- Dispute type is the one that gets fuzzy — you've already hit overlaps. If it's the spine of your system, every ambiguous case becomes a judgment call. If it's just a column in the log, you can list two types for a messy case and move on.

For the folders with no year: use the date of the latest document inside (settlement agreement, closing letter, last correspondence) as a stand-in, and mark it in the log as "approx." rather than guessing silently. If there's truly nothing dated, park them in an "undated — needs review" section at the end instead of forcing them somewhere.

One thing worth doing before you get too deep: ask Gary how he actually goes looking for a closed file. "Do you think 'that 2019 thing' or 'that landlord-tenant thing'?" Thirty seconds of his time saves you redoing the whole log.

**The front desk thing:** I get why that's nagging at you — a bad phone day followed by a back-room task feels like a pattern even when it might not be. Two things to hold at once: it's possible he's giving you some distance from the phones for a day, *and* it's possible he just had an incomplete log that's been bugging him and you were available. From the outside those look identical.

If it keeps chewing at you, ask him directly and lightly — something like "Hey, after yesterday I want to make sure I'm solid on the phone stuff. Anything you want me to do differently?" That gets you an answer without making it a whole thing, and it signals you noticed and care, which is usually what a manager actually wants to see after a rough day. Either way, a clean, well-organized catalog is not a bad thing to hand him this week.

Yeah year as primary makes sense. Ill pull latest doc dates for the missing years and flag the undated ones.

The phone thing though. He brought me tea and said my handwriting is neat That sounds like someone easing you into data entry not a punishment right

Ha — yeah, that's not what benching looks like. Managers who are quietly sidelining someone don't bring them tea. They get vague and busy. Tea plus a compliment on the specific skill the task needs is pretty much the "I picked you for this on purpose" combo.

And "your handwriting is neat" is a real reason to hand someone a cataloging job, not a consolation prize. It means he expects this log to be read later, probably by him, and he wants it done by someone careful.

Could yesterday's phone stuff still be on his mind a little? Sure, maybe. But the read here is "person who's good at detail work gets detail work," not "person who fumbled gets hidden." If anything he's shown you where he thinks you're strong. Take the win, do a clean job on the binders, and the phones will still be there next week.

I get it. So cataloging is actually a sign he trusts me with detail work not a punishment for the phone stuff. That helps. Still feels weird sitting back here while everyone else is at the front desk though.

One more thing the binders have some cases split across two topics like a landlord tenant dispute that also involves a neighbor noise complaint. Do I file that under the primary topic or make a cross-reference note

The sitting-in-the-back feeling is real, and it doesn't have to mean anything for it to still feel a bit isolating. Being physically away from the group for a day is just weird, especially when you're new-ish. That'll fade once you're back on rotation. If it helps, take your breaks up front so you're not invisible all day.

**The split-topic cases:** file under the primary topic, add a cross-reference note. Don't try to make the physical folder live in two places — that's how binders go missing.

How to decide primary: whatever the *mediation itself* was actually about. In your example, if the parties to the mediation were the landlord and tenant, and the noise complaint was the underlying grievance, that's a landlord-tenant case with a noise angle. If the neighbor was actually a party at the table, it's more of a neighbor dispute. Basically: who signed the agreement (or sat in the room) tells you the primary type.

For the log itself, since year is your spine, this is easy — give each entry a "Type" column and a "Secondary/Related" column. Landlord-tenant goes in Type, noise/neighbor goes in Secondary. Anyone searching the log by either topic will still find it, and you're not agonizing over a single box.

Keep a running list of the ones you had to make a call on, too — five or six "I filed this as X, could arguably be Y" lines you can show Gary at the end. Takes him a minute to review, saves you from second-guessing each one in the moment, and is exactly the kind of thing that makes a manager think "this person is careful."

Primary topic with a cross reference note Got it. That landlord tenant example helps a lot actually.

One last thing. If I finish these binders by 4 and have a clean log plus a short list of the edge cases for Gary to review is that enough to show I can handle more than filing

Yes — that's a strong day's work, and it shows the things that actually matter more than filing speed: you noticed gaps, you made reasonable calls, you flagged the ones you weren't sure about instead of guessing, and you didn't need hand-holding. That's the profile of someone you can hand the next unclear task to.

Two small things that turn "good job" into "give this person more":

- **When you hand it over, spend 60 seconds telling him how you organized it**, not just that it's done. "Year primary, type as a column, undated ones flagged at the end, and here are six I wasn't sure about." That's the difference between "she finished the filing" and "she built a system."
- **Don't oversell it or ask for more in the same breath.** Just deliver clean work and let it land. If there's a natural opening later — "if you've got anything else like this, I'm happy to take it" — great. But the work speaks louder than the pitch.

And for what it's worth, one clean day doesn't prove everything, and it doesn't need to. It proves the next thing, and the next thing is what gets you the next thing. That's genuinely how this works.

Alright so year primary with a secondary type column and cross reference notes for the split cases. 4pm delivery with an edge case list sounds doable.

I think I was overthinking the Gary thing. Tea and neat handwriting is probably just what it looks like.

You've got it. That's the whole plan, and it's a good one.

And yeah, tea and a compliment is almost always just tea and a compliment. Overthinking it after a rough phone day is pretty normal — that's your brain trying to get ahead of a problem that isn't there. Nothing wrong with noticing it and setting it down.

Go build a log Gary can actually use. If any weird edge cases pop up that don't fit the landlord-tenant logic, come back and we'll sort them out.
